notes.meaning: God gives Jeremiah a series of messages directed to the foreign nations surrounding Judah. Up to this point, the prophet focused mainly on warning God's own people, but now the Lord speaks to the wider world. The Lord shows that He rules over every empire, not just Israel. No nation on earth is outside of His authority.

This message concerns Pharaoh Neco and the Egyptian army stationed at Carchemish on the Euphrates River. Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon crushed this army in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim of Judah. The defeat proved that Egypt could never be a dependable protector for the people of Jerusalem.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verses 3-12 are a song written after the battle, not a prediction made before it. Keil and Delitzsch argue that it is a true prophecy.

notes.meaning: A call goes out to ready the large body shields and the smaller bucklers for battle. The words picture an army getting organized and marching proudly toward the front line. In reality, God is setting the stage to show how quickly their military pride will fall apart.

Soldiers are told to harness the horses, mount their chariots, put on helmets, polish their spears, and strap on their body armor. Egypt was renowned across the ancient world for its powerful chariots and swift steeds. Yet even the finest weapons cannot save an army when God plans its defeat.

The prophet watches in astonishment as Egypt's confident troops suddenly panic and run. The battle collapses so fast that the soldiers flee in a rush without daring to glance behind them. God surrounds them with terror on every side.

Neither the fastest runners nor the strongest warriors can escape this disaster. Far to the north, along the banks of the Euphrates River, the Egyptian forces trip and fall. Human strength and speed are completely useless when God decides the outcome.

The Lord asks who is advancing like the Nile River when it floods its banks. Egypt marched northward with a huge army that looked like surging waters ready to swallow everything in its path. This image compares their swelling pride to the famous yearly flood of their homeland river.

Egypt answers the question by boasting that it will rise like a flood to cover the earth. Pharaoh bragged that his army would wipe out cities and destroy everyone living in them. But human arrogance is hollow when it challenges the purpose of God.

The commanders urge their war horses to charge, their chariots to race wildly, and their allied troops to advance. Soldiers from Cush and Put carried large shields, while archers from Lydia drew their bows. Even with these seasoned foreign helpers, Egypt cannot alter the defeat ahead.

This day does not belong to Pharaoh, but to the Lord God of Hosts as a day of justice against His enemies. The Lord views the slaughter of the Egyptian army as a sacrifice offered beside the Euphrates River. God brings down those who have long oppressed others and refused to honor Him.

Egypt is mockingly told to travel to the region of Gilead to search for its famous healing ointment. She can try every medicine known, but her political wound is far too deep to be healed. When God brings down an empire, no earthly cure can restore its power.

Neighboring nations hear of Egypt's humiliating overthrow, and her wailing fills the land. In the wild rush to escape, Egyptian soldiers crash into each other and fall together in heaps. Their former glory is shattered for all the world to see.

A second prophecy begins here, warning that King Nebuchadnezzar will actually invade Egypt itself. The first battle at Carchemish stopped Egypt at its border, but this message announces judgment within their own cities. God makes sure that those who trust in earthly strongholds will find no safety there.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historians once doubted that Nebuchadnezzar ever invaded Egypt. Later, an inscription and Babylonian records were found that describe a campaign in his 37th year (about 568-567 BC).

notes.meaning: The alarm is sounded across key Egyptian cities, including Migdol, Memphis, and Tahpanhes. These were the frontier towns where Jewish refugees had fled to hide, against God's direct command. The surrounding countries have already fallen to Babylon, and now Egypt's turn has arrived.

The prophet asks why Egypt's mighty warriors have been swept away like mud in a flash flood. They could not stand firm because the Lord Himself shoved them down. No army can hold its ground when God fights against it.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The old Greek translation reads, "Why did Apis flee?" Apis was Egypt's sacred bull-god. Many scholars follow this reading, so the verse shows Israel's God beating Egypt's god. Keil and Delitzsch do not accept it.

notes.meaning: The Lord causes the defenders to trip and fall over one another in total confusion. Foreign workers and hired soldiers realize the battle is lost and urge each other to head back home. Escaping the sword of judgment requires turning to God rather than looking for a new hiding place.

The fleeing soldiers mock Pharaoh as nothing more than a loud noise who lets the right moment pass him by. He talked boldly about his strength, but he failed to deliver when the test came. Earthly leaders make huge promises, but they cannot save anyone from God's hand.

The true King, whose name is the Lord of Hosts, swears by His own life that the Babylonian conqueror will arrive. Nebuchadnezzar will stand out over Egypt just as Mount Tabor towers over the valley and Mount Carmel overlooks the sea. What God promises under oath is certain to take place.

The people of Egypt are warned to pack their bags for a long march into exile. The great city of Memphis will be completely destroyed and left without anyone living in it. Ancient wealth and famous cities offer no protection when judgment falls.

Egypt is compared to a beautiful, well-fed young cow living in luxury and ease. But a stinging fly, representing the Babylonian army, comes swooping in from the north to torment her. A nation's comfort and ease cannot keep away the trouble God sends.

The hired mercenaries in Egypt lived like fattened calves, but they prove useless in the day of battle. Instead of holding their ground, they turn their backs and run away together. Hired help will never risk its life when God brings the time of punishment.

Egypt can only hiss softly like a scared snake slithering away into the weeds to hide. Her enemies march in with battle-axes like woodcutters ready to chop down trees. A once-proud empire is reduced to quiet groans before an unstoppable foe.

The Babylonian invaders chop down Egypt's towns and leaders just as woodmen clear a thick forest. The invading soldiers are too many to count, covering the land like an endless swarm of locusts. Even the largest population cannot resist God's appointed judgment.

The proud kingdom of Egypt is covered in disgrace and handed over to the people of the north. The Chaldeans capture her land and take her people captive. God humbles those who exalt themselves above His authority.

The God of Israel declares that He will punish Amon, the famous ram-god of Thebes, along with Pharaoh and all Egypt's idols and rulers. He will also judge anyone who puts their trust in Pharaoh instead of the Lord. Depending on false gods or human rulers always leads to disappointment and loss.

God hands Egypt over to Nebuchadnezzar and his royal officers to be conquered. Yet the Lord also promises that Egypt will be inhabited again in later years, just as it was long ago. Even when God brings harsh discipline, He remembers mercy and sets limits to destruction.

The Lord tells His servant Jacob not to be terrified, even while great empires fall all around. He promises to rescue His people and their children from the lands of their captivity and bring them home to live in quiet and safety. God never forgets His people, no matter how far away they have been scattered.

differ.view: The Jewish nation as a nation has ended, but this promise finds its full meaning in the gospel church. The church is God's spiritual Israel, and He will never bring it to an end.
The Jews have survived as a distinct people while their old enemies vanished. This is a sign that Israel will one day be restored to God's favor, when the time of the Gentiles is fulfilled.
The promise of a peaceful return looks ahead to a future kingdom age for Israel that has not come yet.

notes.meaning: The Lord repeats His comfort to Jacob, reminding them that He is with them. He will bring a total end to the heathen nations where they were exiled, but He will not wipe out Israel. Instead, He will discipline His people justly so that they may be corrected and restored.
